unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6! This unit is all about sports, the Olympics, and what it means to achieve something great. You will explore how athletes train, how the Olympic Games began in ancient Greece, and how the Paralympics have changed our understanding of what the human body can do. Along the way you will build powerful vocabulary, strengthen your grammar, and learn to write about sports with confidence and skill.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the Vocabulary companion and learn the thirty unit words a few at a time, saying each example aloud. Work through the Grammar companion: compound nouns, abstract nouns, indefinite pronouns, comparative adverbs and ways of expressing the future. Read The Spirit of the Olympics and A Day in the Life of a Young Athlete, then the two-part story The Truth in the Margins, answering the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Complete the grammar practice, the sports profile, match report and comparison writing tasks, and the debate, presentation and interview speaking tasks, then finish with the quiz and the Check Your Learning self-assessment.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A suggestion that is not stated directly but can be understood.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The implication of the new fitness data was that the squad needed longer recovery periods.
practiceSentences: The implication of the new fitness data was that the squad needed longer recovery periods.
What is the implication for smaller schools if the league raises its entry fees again?
"The implication of your silence," said the captain quietly, "is that you disagree with the plan."
I resented the implication that our team had won only because the referee favoured us.
An implication is carried by a statement; an inference is drawn by a listener.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The act of becoming better, or making something better than before.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Real improvement often comes from small, steady changes rather than one big leap.
practiceSentences: Real improvement often comes from small, steady changes rather than one big leap.
Has there been any improvement in her sprint times this season?
The coach measured improvement in seconds, not in effort.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A new method or idea put into practice.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The clap-skate was an innovation that rewrote the record books.
practiceSentences: The clap-skate was an innovation that rewrote the record books.
What innovation changed this sport most?
An innovation is an idea that has actually been used.
Their innovation was a training schedule, not a machine.
An invention is made; an innovation is adopted.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The particular way something is understood or explained.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The referee's interpretation of the rule decided the match.
practiceSentences: The referee's interpretation of the rule decided the match.
What interpretation would you offer of this result?
An interpretation is a reading, and other readings exist.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Giving a vaccine so the body can build immunity in advance.

practiceSentences: Vaccination is required before travelling to some tournaments.
Why does vaccination protect people who cannot be vaccinated?
Vaccination trains the immune system without the illness.
The squad completed its vaccination two months before the games.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A graph that plots two measurements against each other.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Chosen with no pattern, so every outcome is equally likely.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Describing the verb form used to state a fact.

practiceSentences: In "she runs every morning", "runs" is indicative.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Describing the form used to ask a question.

practiceSentences: "Who", "what" and "which" are interrogative words.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A true account of part of the writer's own life.

practiceSentences: Her memoir covers only the year she spent at sea.

practiceSentences: The editorial argued for a safer crossing.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words: kinds of writing and how they read

readings.title: The Spirit of the Olympics
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every four years, athletes from around the world gather for the Olympic Games. The event is a celebration of sport, hard work, and human achievement. But the story of the Olympics stretches back thousands of years, to a time when ancient Greece hosted the very first competitions in a place called Olympia.
The ancient Games began around 776 BCE. At first, there was only one race — a short sprint called the stadion. Over time, the Greeks added wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, and the pentathlon. Athletes trained for months. Winning brought enormous honour, not just to the individual but to the athlete’s entire city-state. There was no silver or bronze in those days; only the winner received the olive wreath. The contrast between ancient and modern ceremonies is striking, yet the spirit of fair competition has remained the same.
The modern Olympics were revived in 1896 by Pierre de Coubertin, a French educator who believed sport could bring nations together. The first modern Games, held in Athens, featured just 241 athletes from 14 countries. Today, the Games welcome over 10,000 competitors from more than 200 nations — a powerful symbol of global diversity.
One of the most important developments in recent decades has been the growth of the Paralympic Games. The Paralympics celebrate athletes with physical disabilities, proving that courage and determination matter far more than physical limitations. Wheelchair basketball, sitting volleyball, and blade running have become some of the most exciting events to watch. An analogy that many coaches use is this: “Ability is like an iceberg — what you see on the surface is only a small part of the whole.”
Yet the world of sport also faces serious challenges. Bias can influence decisions made by judges and officials. Doping — the use of banned substances to improve performance — threatens fair play. Some critics argue that hosting the Games costs too much money and that ordinary citizens rarely benefit. These are not easy problems, and people hold different viewpoints about how to solve them.
Despite these challenges, the Olympic movement continues to inspire. When a young athlete from a small village stands on the podium, the message is clear: with discipline, training, and a strong objective, extraordinary things are possible. The evidence is in every record broken, every personal best achieved, and every handshake between competitors who moments earlier were rivals.
Sport teaches us that success is not inevitable — it must be earned through effort and perseverance. Whether you play football in a dusty field or swim laps in an Olympic pool, the lessons are the same: set a goal, work hard, respect your opponents, and never stop improving. That is the true spirit of the Olympics, and it belongs to everyone.

readings.title: A Day in the Life of a Young Athlete
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Sana wakes at five o'clock every morning, even at weekends. Before the sun rises over Hargeisa, she is already stretching on the dusty road outside her home. Running is more than a hobby for Sana — it is her objective, her daily commitment, and the one thing that makes her feel truly alive.
Her training routine is strict. She runs eight kilometres before breakfast, rests during the hottest part of the day, and then does strength exercises in the afternoon. Her coach, a former national athlete, watches her progress carefully and keeps a training log so they can estimate how fast she is improving each month. "Numbers are evidence of hard work," he tells her. "They don't lie."
Sana's dream is to compete at the East African Schools Championships. She knows the competition will be fierce — runners from Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Ethiopia train just as hard as she does. But she is not discouraged. "My mother always says that nothing worth having comes easily," Sana explains. "When I feel tired, I remember that every step forward is a step closer to my goal."
Not everything is easy. Sana sometimes struggles to balance training with her schoolwork. She misses social events because she has to sleep early. Some classmates do not understand why she works so hard. But her resolution is firm: she will represent her country one day. For Sana, achievement is not about medals alone. It is about proving to herself that discipline and determination can overcome any obstacle.
Last year, Sana entered her first regional trial. She finished fourth, two seconds outside the qualifying time, and sat in silence for most of the bus ride home. Her coach refused to treat the defeat as a disaster. From his viewpoint, the result was simply more evidence for the training log — proof of exactly how far she still had to travel. "Fourth place is not a failure," he told her the next morning. "It is an estimate of the distance between today and your dream. Now we know the size of the work ahead."
Since that day, Sana has adjusted her routine in small, deliberate ways. She sleeps earlier, records every session in her own notebook beside the coach's official log, and studies how champion runners pace the final laps of their races. When younger children in her neighbourhood ask why she runs before sunrise, she gives them the same answer every time: improvement is never inevitable — it is a choice you make again each morning. Her story is far from finished, and the road ahead is longer than the road behind her, but everyone who watches her train along that dusty street before dawn believes exactly the same thing: the next regional trial is going to tell a very different story.

readings.title: The Truth in the Margins, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
“Everyone is talking about it,” said Rohan, sliding his tray onto the lunch table. “Did you see the new story in the school magazine?”
Amara looked up. “No. What’s it about?”
Rohan lowered his voice. “It’s a piece about exam cheating — but it blames the Form 3 students. People are angry. They say it’s full of bias.”
Amara blinked. She was the editor of The Beacon, the school’s monthly publication. As far as she knew, no article like that had been approved. She stood up and walked straight to the notice board.
There it was: a stapled page titled “The Downfall of Discipline.”
She read quickly. The article claimed that cheating had become inevitable, and it made sharp comparisons between current students and “the golden classes of the past.” There was a dramatic climax accusing one entire stream of “undermining the school’s values.”
“No name. No byline,” she murmured. “But it’s written like an opinion piece. And it’s not neutral.”
The problem wasn’t just the anger. It was the structure. The article mixed opinion and fact with no clear introduction or logical organisation. Worse, it didn’t use proper evidence. It quoted unnamed sources and offered no balance in viewpoint.
By afternoon, students from Form 3 were yelling in the corridor. One group accused the editorial team of targeting them. Another group defended the piece, saying it was an “honest reflection.”
That evening, Amara called a meeting in the journalism room. Everyone on the team came — except Zara, the assistant editor.
“I didn’t publish that,” Amara said. “It wasn’t part of the approved structure.”
“Then how did it get printed?” Rohan asked.
Amara paused. “We only printed five copies. Someone added a sixth.”
Rohan frowned. “So someone illustrated their opinion with false facts.”
“It’s more serious than that,” Amara said. “It could damage our school’s unity. The implication is that a whole group is dishonest.”
The next morning, the head teacher summoned her. “This has become a judicial matter within the school. The article sparked complaints. You need to respond.”
Amara nodded. “We’re preparing a public resolution. And I want to publish a follow-up article that explains the context.”
The head teacher tapped his pen. “Just be careful. More damage could happen if the issue isn’t handled more objectively.”
Back at the newsroom, the team argued over what to do next. One writer said, “Let’s write an angry reply. Expose whoever did it.”
Rohan shook his head. “That’s just argumentative for no reason. We need to think.”
Amara took a deep breath. “We should focus on explaining the process. Use facts. Include quotations. And explore multiple viewpoints.”
“We’ll write a new piece,” she said, “called The Truth in the Margins. It’ll have a clear introduction, supported by real evidence, and offer alternative voices. It’ll ask questions instead of blaming.”

readings.title: The Truth in the Margins, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
They began the next day. Amara gathered real accounts from students, teachers, and prefects. Rohan wrote an excerpt about the history of cheating incidents. They included a summary of school rules and policies and made sure each paragraph had proper organisation.
“I’ll also add a section about censorship,” Rohan said. “So readers understand why unofficial publications matter.”
Zara arrived at the newsroom midweek, red-faced and silent. After a long pause, she whispered, “I added the article. I thought it would create discussion.”
Amara stared at her. “But without approval?”
“I’m sorry,” Zara said. “I just wanted to raise the issue. I didn’t expect it to spread.”
Amara could have been angry. But she saw something in Zara’s face — fear and regret.
“We can’t undo it,” she said. “But we can illustrate the bigger issue. Why did you feel unheard?”
Zara’s eyes welled. “I felt like no one was acknowledging the real pressure we’re under. We act like everything’s fine, but it’s not.”
The team sat quietly. Then Rohan said, “Maybe that’s the real story.”
They added a new section: Behind the Panic: Student Voices. It showed anonymous student reflections on stress, comparing the pressure now to earlier years. They used an analogy: “Stress is like a rope. The more you pull, the more likely it snaps.”
They also estimated that over 80% of senior students worried about exams daily.
The piece included proper structure, used neutral language, and had diverse perspectives. One line read: “Some believe discipline has dwindled; others say expectations have changed. The truth may lie in the contrast.”
On Friday, they published the corrected edition.
The school read it during form time. It did not cause a riot. It caused reflection.
One teacher said, “It’s far more concisely written than the first.”
Another said, “It’s balanced. I see no bias.”
Zara was not punished. But she did write a short note in the next issue, acknowledging the importance of proper publishing process.
Over the next weeks, students submitted more writing — essays about resilience, opinion pieces about uniform rules, even poems about exam fear.
Rohan grinned. “Our next edition is going to be big.”
Amara smiled. “And far less chaotic.”
At the end of the term, The Beacon was nominated for a regional schools writing award.
As they gathered for the celebration, Amara reflected: organisation, truth, and diversity don’t just make good stories — they build strong communities.
In a world where censorship, bias, and disconnection can spread quickly, storytelling had become their tool for clarity.
And in the margin of that moment, truth had finally found its voice.

grammar.title: Compound Nouns
grammar.explanation: A compound noun combines two or more words to make a new noun with its own specific meaning, such as goalkeeper, team-mate and swimming pool. The language of sport is full of them, so recognising the three written forms makes your writing precise.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: There are three forms. Closed form joins the words with no space: football, goalkeeper, scoreboard, teamwork. Hyphenated form joins them with a hyphen: team-mate, runner-up, half-time. Open form keeps two separate words that work as one noun: swimming pool, world record, starting line. The first word usually describes or limits the second: in football, foot tells you what kind of ball game it is, and in world record, world tells you the scale of the record.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing a closed compound with a space (goal keeper instead of goalkeeper) or dropping the hyphen from a hyphenated one (runner up instead of runner-up). When you are unsure which form a compound takes, check a dictionary before you submit your work.
grammar.memoryTip: Compound nouns are team players: two words pass to each other and score one new meaning together.
grammar.practice:
Part A — identify the compound noun in each sentence and label it closed, hyphenated or open: 1) The goalkeeper saved three shots during the match. 2) She broke the world record in the sprint. 3) Our team-mate scored the winning goal. 4) The swimming pool was closed for repairs. 5) Good teamwork helped them win the tournament. Part B — build a compound noun from each pair and use it in a sentence of your own: score + board, basket + ball, half + time, starting + line, sports + man + ship. Part C — complete each sentence with the compound formed from the brackets: 6) I need a new (tooth + brush) because mine is old. 7) Check the (score + board) to see who is winning. 8) The (goal + keeper) made an incredible save in the last minute. 9) The (swimming + pool) at our school is twenty-five metres long. 10) The (half + time) break gave the team a chance to rest.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: (1) goalkeeper — closed (2) world record — open (3) team-mate — hyphenated (4) swimming pool — open (5) teamwork — closed.
Part B: score + board = scoreboard (closed); basket + ball = basketball (closed); half + time = half-time (hyphenated); starting + line = starting line (open); sports + man + ship = sportsmanship (closed). The sentences you write with each compound are open-ended — self-check model: "The scoreboard showed our team was winning." Check that your sentence uses the compound naturally and spells it in its correct form (closed, hyphenated or open).
Part C: (6) toothbrush (7) scoreboard (8) goalkeeper (9) swimming pool (10) half-time.

grammar.title: Abstract Nouns
grammar.explanation: An abstract noun names something you cannot see, touch or hold: an idea, a feeling, a quality or a state. Words like courage, achievement and diversity let you write about the values of sport, not just its equipment.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Most abstract nouns are built from adjectives, verbs or other nouns with a suffix: happy becomes happiness, diverse becomes diversity, brave becomes bravery, organise becomes organisation, resolve becomes resolution, achieve becomes achievement, friend becomes friendship, child becomes childhood. Watch for the signal suffixes -ness, -ity, -ry, -tion, -ment, -ship and -hood. Compare the two kinds of noun: you can hold a medal or a trophy in your hands, but you cannot hold courage, fairness or perseverance.
grammar.commonMistake: Using the adjective or verb where the noun belongs: the brave of the athlete should be the bravery of the athlete, and the organise was good should be the organisation was good. Check that the word's form matches its job in the sentence.
grammar.memoryTip: If you can feel it or think it but cannot put it in your kit bag, it is probably an abstract noun.
grammar.practice:

Part B — sort these ten words into concrete nouns you can touch and abstract nouns you cannot: medal, courage, trophy, fairness, stadium, ambition, whistle, perseverance, track, friendship.

grammar.title: Pronouns — Everyone, Someone, Anyone
grammar.explanation: Everyone, someone and anyone are indefinite pronouns: they refer to people in a general way without naming anybody. Although each one can describe many people, English treats them all as singular.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use everyone for all the people in a group: Everyone is excited about the match. Use someone for one unknown person: Someone left a water bottle on the pitch. Use anyone for any person at all: Anyone can join the training session. Because these pronouns are singular, they always take singular verbs: Everyone is happy. Someone has a question. Anyone who wants to play needs to sign up.
grammar.commonMistake: Pairing an indefinite pronoun with a plural verb, as in Everyone are ready. The pronoun points to many people, but the verb must stay singular: Everyone is ready.
grammar.memoryTip: Treat everyone as one single team rather than as its many players: everyone is, never everyone are.
grammar.practice:
Choose everyone, someone or anyone, then pick the correct verb form: 1) ____ in the stadium (was / were) cheering for the home team. 2) ____ (has / have) forgotten a sports kit in the changing room. 3) ____ who wants to play in the tournament (need / needs) to sign up today. 4) ____ on the team (deserve / deserves) a medal for such effort.

=== Answer Key ===
(1) Everyone ... was (2) Someone ... has (3) Anyone ... needs (4) Everyone ... deserves. Self-check: everyone/someone/anyone are always singular, so pair each with the singular verb form (is/was, has, needs, deserves), never the plural (are/were, have, need, deserve).

grammar.title: Comparative Adverbs
grammar.explanation: Comparative adverbs compare how two actions are done: who ran faster, who defended more calmly, who played better. Sports writing leans on them constantly, so forming them accurately makes every report sharper.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Short adverbs of one syllable add -er: fast becomes faster and hard becomes harder. Longer adverbs, usually ending in -ly, take more or less: quickly becomes more quickly and carefully becomes less carefully. Irregular forms must be memorised: well becomes better, badly becomes worse, far becomes further. Always complete the comparison with than: She runs faster than her opponent.
grammar.commonMistake: Doubling the comparative (more faster) or leaving out than. She runs more quickly is unfinished until you add the second half: She runs more quickly than her friend.
grammar.memoryTip: More or less, it is a test: long adverbs take more or less, while short adverbs simply add -er.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the comparative form of the adverb in brackets: 1) Amal sprints (fast) than anyone else on the team. 2) The goalkeeper reacted (quickly) in the second half than in the first. 3) Our school team played (well) this season than last season. 4) He throws the javelin (far) than all the other competitors. 5) The referee explained the rules (clearly) the second time. Part B — rewrite each pair as a single comparison: 6) Leo trains with great effort; Sami trains with less effort. Begin: Leo trains... 7) The swimmer completed her second lap at higher speed than her first. Begin: She swam... 8) Maya spoke about her race confidently; Nora spoke less confidently. Begin: Maya spoke... Part C — two more to finish: 9) My brother plays video games (skilfully) than I do. 10) She explained the tactics (thoroughly) than the assistant coach.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: (1) faster (2) more quickly (3) better (4) further (5) more clearly.
Part B (model rewrites — exact wording may vary, but the comparative form and than must both appear): (6) Leo trains harder than Sami. (7) She swam faster in her second lap than in her first. (8) Maya spoke more confidently than Nora.
Part C: (9) more skilfully (10) more thoroughly.

grammar.title: Expressing the Future
grammar.explanation: English has three main ways to talk about the future, and each carries a slightly different meaning: instant decisions and predictions, plans already made, and fixed arrangements.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use will + base verb for predictions, promises and decisions made at the moment of speaking: I will train harder this season. The match will start at three o'clock. Use be going to + base verb for plans already made and predictions based on evidence: She is going to compete in the national championships. Look at those clouds — it is going to rain during the match. Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements in the near future: We are playing against Hillside School tomorrow. The coach is arriving at noon.
grammar.commonMistake: Using will for a plan that is already settled. Saying I will go to practice on Friday suggests you are deciding right now; once the plan is fixed, prefer I am going to go to practice on Friday.
grammar.memoryTip: Will is a promise, going to is a plan, and the present continuous is a diary entry already written in your calendar.
grammar.practice:
Complete each sentence with will, a form of be going to, or the present continuous form of the verb in brackets, and be ready to explain your choice: 1) I ____ (write) my match report this weekend, because I have already planned it. 2) She ____ (present) her research on the Olympics next Monday; the date is fixed. 3) We ____ (discuss) the results in our next lesson. 4) They ____ (finish) their training before the tournament begins.

=== Answer Key ===
(1) am going to write — a plan already made ("because I have already planned it"). (2) is presenting — a fixed arrangement ("the date is fixed"). (3) will discuss — a prediction/decision with no clue of a pre-arranged plan. (4) will finish — a prediction, not a diarised arrangement. Self-check: look for the signal words in each sentence — "already planned" points to going to, "date is fixed" points to the present continuous, and no such signal defaults to will.

grammar.title: Grade 7 Editing and Application
grammar.explanation: Strong writers pull the whole unit together: they check compound nouns, abstract nouns, comparative adverbs, pronoun agreement and future forms while revising a complete paragraph for meaning and flow.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Read your draft aloud one sentence at a time. Check that every compound noun uses its correct written form, every abstract noun matches its job in the sentence, every comparison includes than, every indefinite pronoun takes a singular verb, and every future form matches the meaning you intend. Revise one feature at a time, then reread the whole paragraph to hear the difference.
grammar.commonMistake: Changing words without checking whether the paragraph still means the same thing. Explain the purpose of every revision to yourself before you accept it.
grammar.memoryTip: Edit like a referee reviewing a replay: one incident at a time, then the whole passage again at full speed.
grammar.practice:
Part A — mixed review: 1) Identify the compound noun in The scoreboard showed the final result and give its form. 2) Name the abstract noun in The crowd admired her courage. 3) Complete with a comparative adverb: The second-place runner finished (close) to the winner than expected. 4) Build a compound noun from basket and ball and label its form. 5) Turn strong into an abstract noun and use it in a sentence about an athlete. 6) Write one sentence comparing two athletes with the comparative form of gracefully. Part B — vocabulary in context: complete each sentence with the best word from this bank — analogy, bias, evidence, viewpoint, objective, resolution, estimate, inevitable, diversity, structure: 7) The coach used an ____ to explain teamwork: a team is like a machine, because every part matters. 8) Her main ____ this season is to qualify for the national championships. 9) The journalist showed ____ by interviewing players from only one team. 10) Scientists found ____ that regular exercise improves concentration. 11) After the disagreement, the two players reached a peaceful ____. 12) The ____ of the Olympic village reflects the many cultures of the world. 13) Experts ____ that over three billion people watched the last opening ceremony. 14) From the coach's ____, the defence needed the most improvement. 15) Losing a match is not ____ if you prepare well and stay focused. 16) The ____ of the article was clear: introduction, evidence, conclusion.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: (1) scoreboard — closed compound noun (2) courage — abstract noun (3) closer ("finished closer to the winner than expected") (4) basketball — closed form (5) strength — the noun form is fixed, but the sentence is open-ended; self-check model: "The athlete showed great strength under pressure." (6) open-ended — self-check model: "Amal moved more gracefully than her rival." Check that you used more gracefully together with than.
Part B: (7) analogy (8) objective (9) bias (10) evidence (11) resolution (12) diversity (13) estimate (14) viewpoint (15) inevitable (16) structure.

writing.title: Writing 1: Letter of Advice to the Editor
writing.promptAndInstructions: After reading The Truth in the Margins, write a letter to Amara, the editor of The Beacon. In 100 to 150 words, give her your advice about how she handled the unauthorised article. Say whether you agree with her decision not to punish Zara, explain your reasons with evidence from the story, and suggest one thing you would have done differently. Open and close your letter politely, and use at least three vocabulary words from this unit.
writing.modelText:
Dear Amara,
I have just finished reading about what happened at The Beacon, and I agree with your decision not to punish Zara. The evidence shows she acted from good intentions, not bias, even though her article lacked proper structure and context. In my viewpoint, one thing I would have done differently is asking Zara to write a short resolution note for the next issue, explaining what she learned.
Yours sincerely,
A reader
writing.sentenceStarter: Dear Amara, I have just finished reading about what happened at The Beacon...
writing.expectedLength: Two organised paragraphs in letter form

items: Dear Amara, I have just finished reading about what happened at The Beacon, and I agree with your decision not to punish Zara. The evidence in the story shows that she acted from good intentions, wanting to expose a real problem, even though her article lacked proper structure and context, which left readers without enough evidence to judge the claims fairly.

In my viewpoint, one thing I would have done differently is asking Zara to write a short resolution note for the next issue, explaining what she learned about checking facts before publishing something so serious. Yours sincerely, A reader

Another learner might propose a middle position: no formal punishment, but a public correction printed in the very next issue so readers know the first article was unreliable.

writing.title: Writing 2: Sports Profile
writing.promptAndInstructions:
A sports profile is a short piece of writing that introduces a sportsperson to the reader. It gives key facts, describes achievements, and includes a personal touch that makes the person come alive on the page.
Choose a sportsperson you admire — a famous international athlete, a local player, or someone from your school or community. Write a sports profile of 200 to 250 words.
Your profile should include:
Introduction: full name, sport, and country or city of origin.
Background: how they started, what inspired them, any challenges they faced.
Achievements: key results, records, awards. Use at least one compound noun (for example world record, team-mate, championship title).
Qualities: what makes them special? Use at least one abstract noun (for example determination, courage, resilience).
Your opinion: why do you admire this person? End with a strong closing sentence.
Model opening (for guidance):
Sana is a long-distance runner from Hargeisa who wakes before sunrise to train on the roads outside her home. Her strict routine and firm resolution have carried her towards the East African Schools Championships, and her determination shows that discipline can overcome any obstacle.
writing.modelText:
Sana is a long-distance runner from Hargeisa who wakes before sunrise to train on the dusty roads outside her home.
She began running as a young girl, inspired by watching older athletes compete at the local school field, and she has faced many challenges, including the heat and long distances to training.
Her greatest achievement is breaking the regional school record, a real championship title that surprised even her coach.
What makes Sana special is her quiet determination, and I admire her because she proves that discipline can overcome any obstacle.
writing.sentenceStarter: The sportsperson I admire most is...

items: Introduction: Ayaan Mohamed is a swimmer from Berbera who trains every morning in the sea before the town fully wakes up.

Background: She began swimming as a young girl, inspired by her older brother who represented their region at a national meet, and she has faced many challenges, including the cost of proper training gear and the long walk to the only pool in town.
Achievements (compound noun): Her greatest achievement is holding the regional freestyle record, a real championship title she earned as the youngest swimmer in the final.

Qualities and opinion (abstract noun): What makes Ayaan special is her quiet determination, and I admire her because she proves that resilience, more than talent alone, is what carries an athlete to the top.

writing.title: Writing 3: Match Report
writing.promptAndInstructions:
A match report describes what happened during a sporting event. It is a type of non-fiction writing that uses clear, factual language with some descriptive detail to bring the event to life.
Think of a match or sporting event you have watched or played in. Write a match report of 200 to 250 words.
Your report should include:
Headline: a short, attention-grabbing title (for example "Eagles Soar to Victory in Thrilling Final").
Opening paragraph: who played? When and where? What was the final result?
Key moments: describe two or three important moments from the match. Use at least one comparative adverb (for example "The striker moved more quickly than the defenders").
Outcome and reaction: how did the match end? How did the players or crowd react?
Closing sentence: a comment on what the result means for the team or the season.
Model opening (for guidance):
On Saturday afternoon, Riverside FC defeated Hillside United 3-1 in a thrilling cup final at the town stadium. The home side started more aggressively than their opponents, and midfielder Kian opened the scoring in the fifteenth minute with a powerful long-range shot.
writing.modelText:
Eagles Soar to Victory in Thrilling Final
On Saturday afternoon, Riverside FC defeated Hillside United 2-1 at the town stadium in front of a noisy crowd.
The home side started more confidently than their opponents, and midfielder Amal scored first with a curling shot in the tenth minute. Hillside fought back quickly, but Riverside's defence held firm until the final whistle.
Fans cheered loudly as the players celebrated together on the pitch.
This win keeps Riverside's hopes alive for the championship title this season.

Outcome and reaction: Supporters roared as the penalty found the net, and players from both sides shook hands warmly despite the tense finish.
Closing sentence: This win keeps Falcons top of the local table with two matches left to play this season.

writing.title: Writing 4: Comparison Paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a paragraph of 100 to 150 words comparing the ancient Olympic Games with the modern Olympic Games. Use the information from the reading passage and your own research to make at least three clear points of comparison.
Your paragraph should:
Begin with a clear topic sentence that introduces the comparison.
Use at least two comparative adverbs (for example more widely, less frequently, better).
Include at least one compound noun (for example city-state, opening ceremony, world record).
End with a sentence explaining which version of the Games you find more interesting and why.
Useful sentence starters for comparisons:
"The ancient Games were organised more simply than the modern Games because..."
"Today, athletes compete more frequently than in ancient times, with events held..."
"While the ancient Olympics featured fewer events, the modern Games include..."
"The opening ceremony is planned more elaborately today than it was in ancient Greece."
writing.modelText: The ancient Olympic Games were organised more simply than the modern Games, with only a handful of events held in one city-state. Today, athletes compete more frequently, travelling the world for a single world record or an Olympic medal, and the opening ceremony is planned far more elaborately than any ancient festival. I find the modern Games more interesting, because so many different countries now share in the same, ancient spirit of competition.
writing.sentenceStarter: The ancient and modern Olympic Games share one spirit but differ in...

items: The ancient Olympic Games were organised more simply than the modern Games, with only a handful of events held in a single city-state every four years. Today, athletes compete more frequently, travelling the world for a single world record or an Olympic medal, and the opening ceremony is planned far more elaborately than any ancient festival ever was. I find the modern Games more interesting, because so many different countries now share in the same ancient spirit of competition that once belonged to one region alone.
otherAnswers: A learner who prefers the ancient Games might argue that their simplicity, held in one sacred place, feels more meaningful than an event spread across a huge modern city.
Another learner might say both versions interest them equally, since the modern Games' scale and the ancient Games' history each tell a different part of the same long story.

writing.title: Writing 5: School Editorial
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you are a student journalist at your own school, like the team behind The Beacon. Write an editorial of about 150 words on an issue that matters to your school community. Our school needs to talk honestly about mobile phones in class. Some teachers argue that phones are a constant distraction, and evidence from our own survey shows that most students check messages during lessons.
Others present a different viewpoint: phones can support learning, offering quick access to dictionaries and research, and banning them entirely feels like an extreme resolution.
In my objective view, a fair compromise is allowing phones only for approved tasks, giving structure to their use instead of confusion.

Others present a different viewpoint: too much homework leaves no time for sport, family or rest, and several students say the pressure has become a genuine source of anxiety rather than motivation. A few teachers privately agree that the current amount is excessive.

In my objective view, a fair resolution is capping homework at forty-five minutes per subject and coordinating deadlines between teachers, giving structure to the workload instead of leaving it to chance.

A learner writing about the school canteen might compare evidence about food waste with student opinions about menu choice, before proposing a compromise.
A learner writing about sports funding might weigh evidence about participation numbers against the school's limited budget.

Improve every piece using the Grade 7 rubrics before submitting: reward clear structure, precise unit vocabulary, evidence for every claim, at least one compound noun and one abstract noun in the profile, and a comparative adverb used with than in the report.
Marking guidance for the teacher. Award the 40 marks as follows. Writing, 16 marks: the four writing rubric criteria — ideas, organisation, language and conventions — four marks each. Speaking, 16 marks: the four speaking rubric criteria — clarity, vocabulary, sentence accuracy and interaction — four marks each. Source annotation, 8 marks: 4 marks for attributing every source used, naming what it is and where it came from, and 4 marks for the comparison or evaluation the task asks for.

quizzes.question: What does 'analogy' mean?
quizzes.options: A difficult or tricky situation. | A way of explaining something by comparing it to something else that is similar. | When authorities control what people can see, read, or say. | The place or point where something begins or comes from.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A way of explaining something by comparing it to something else that is similar.
quizzes.explanation: An analogy explains by comparing: the teacher used an analogy to explain how a computer works by comparing it to a brain.

quizzes.question: What does 'predicament' mean?
quizzes.options: A firm decision or promise to do something. | A short part taken from a longer piece of writing. | A difficult or tricky situation. | A connection or relationship with a group or organisation.
quizzes.explanation: A predicament is a tricky situation: when the goalkeeper was injured, the team was in a real predicament.

quizzes.question: What does 'judicial' mean?
quizzes.options: Related to courts of law and judges. | Expected or likely to happen in the future. | Certain to happen and impossible to avoid. | Aware of and able to think about what is happening.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Related to courts of law and judges.
quizzes.explanation: Judicial describes anything connected with courts and judges, as in the judicial system that ensures rules are followed fairly.

quizzes.question: What does 'implication' mean?
quizzes.options: The difference between two things when you compare them. | The presence of many different types of people or things. | The way something is built or organised. | A suggestion that is not stated directly but can be understood.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A suggestion that is not stated directly but can be understood.
quizzes.explanation: An implication is understood without being said: the implication of his words was that the team needed to train harder.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Sports, Olympics, and Achievement" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 11-12 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'analogy'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Read and understand non-fiction texts about sports and the Olympic Games.
Use important vocabulary such as analogy, bias, evidence, viewpoint, and more.
Recognise and form compound nouns (e.g. football, swimming pool, team-mate).
Identify abstract nouns that name ideas and feelings (e.g. courage, achievement, diversity).
Compare actions using comparative adverbs (e.g. more quickly, less carefully, better).
Write a sports profile and a match report using clear structure and lively detail.
Speak confidently about sports topics, present research, and discuss ethical questions.
Think critically about inclusion, fairness, and achievement in sport.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "The Spirit of the Olympics" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Truth in the Margins, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Compound Nouns" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
